conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad we have a chance to speak today. My name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a tool to help us check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past week so we can make sure you’re getting the support you need. Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space—there are no right or wrong answers, only what’s true for you. We’ll go through ten gentle questions, and we can pause anytime you like. Ready to begin?

Thinking about the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly... I can still laugh sometimes, but it feels like I have to remind myself to. Like, my husband cracked a joke yesterday and I did chuckle, but it didn’t come as easily as it used to. I’d say most days I manage a smile, but it’s not that natural, belly-laugh feeling I remember before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’d say… sometimes. There are moments I can laugh, like when my older sister sent that silly meme, but it doesn’t last long. Mostly I feel like I’m faking it so people won’t worry.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like our weekly stroller walk with the neighbor moms—but when the time comes I just feel… flat. I still go, and once I’m there it’s okay, but that eager “can’t-wait” feeling I used to get doesn’t really show up anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I do catch myself doing that—like last night when the baby wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking I must’ve eaten something to upset her, or that I’m just not doing something right. It’s not every time, but yeah, a few days a week I hear that little voice saying it’s probably my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty often. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure something’s wrong with the baby—even though she’s right there, breathing fine. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t shake the “what-if” thoughts. It happens maybe every other day, sometimes more.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a tight-chest moment that comes out of nowhere—like I’m standing at the changing table and suddenly feel I can’t catch my breath. It passes in a few minutes, but it’s unsettling because nothing actually triggered it.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between the night feeds, the constant laundry, and trying to remember if I’ve eaten, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I keep ticking things off the list, but the list just grows, and by evening I’m exhausted and teary.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week I’ve lain there with my mind racing—going over every little thing I might’ve done wrong or worrying something will happen to the baby—and I just can’t drift off even when she’s sound asleep. It’s not every night, but it’s enough that I feel even more drained the next day.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I’d say a lot of the time. It’s not constant, but most days there’s this heavy, sad cloud that sits on me. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason, or I’ll look at her and instead of pure joy I just feel… empty and guilty that I’m not happier.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not a ton—maybe once or twice this week. It’s usually when I’m already worn out and the baby won’t nap; I’ll end up in the rocker with tears rolling down, but it’s not an everyday thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I feel overwhelmed and tired, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

Your heartfelt description paints a picture of a mum who loves her baby and is working tirelessly, yet most days feel weighed down by a heavy, joyless cloud. Between the endless feeds, self-doubt, sudden waves of panic, and nights spent wide-eyed with racing thoughts, you're running on empty while still showing up for your child-an effort that is both admirable and clearly exhausting.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 20, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional laughter that feels forced and fleeting, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a notable loss of anticipatory enjoyment—"that eager can't-wait feeling" is absent—matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blaming "a few days a week", which aligns with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, irrational worries occurring "every other day, sometimes more," matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic-like episodes (tight chest, breathlessness) that occur "sometimes" without triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" with multiple stressors (feeds, laundry, exhaustion) and inability to keep up, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple nights of racing thoughts preventing sleep due to unhappiness, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "a lot of the time" and "most days", aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS item scores total 20 (≥14 indicates probable postpartum depression). Key endorsements map to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, fatigue, inappropriate guilt, recurrent panic-like anxiety, and insomnia. The patient's quotes (<quote>feel like I'm faking it</quote>, <quote>sad cloud that sits on me</quote>) plus functional impairment (difficulty coping, evening teariness) further support this level of concern. No self-harm ideation (Q10 score 0) is reassuring. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental health specialist for full evaluation and treatment planning
2. Continue or start evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or interpersonal therapy tailored for postpartum depression
3. Screen for thyroid dysfunction and anemia; review medications and physical health
4. Enlist practical help (partner, family, doula) for night feeds/household tasks to improve sleep and reduce overload
5. Practice daily 10-minute self-care (shower, short walk, light snack) and brief paced breathing when panic sensations arise
6. Schedule EPDS re-screen within two weeks to monitor progress
7. Maintain emergency contacts: 24-hr helpline, local urgent mental health service, and inform your support network of warning signs to watch for
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 20: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (self-report)

Symptoms/observations endorsed:  
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness, anhedonia (“flat,” no “can’t-wait” feeling)  
- Daily sense of being overwhelmed, “one step behind,” evening teariness  
- Unwarranted self-blame several days/week (“must’ve eaten something…”)  
- Unexplained episodic anxiety/panic (heart racing, chest tightness, breathlessness) ~ every other day  
- Initial insomnia secondary to racing worries; occurring multiple nights/week  
- Denies any self-harm ideation

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning and enjoyment of infant; no safety concerns voiced.

Screening significance:  
High endorsement for probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; meets threshold for further evaluation (Edinburgh score likely ≥12; items 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 positive; item 10 negative).

Risk factors: mood-linked sleep loss, guilt cognitions, recurrent panic-like episodes, functional overload.

Recommendation: Refer for comprehensive clinical assessment to rule in/out Major Depressive Episode with Anxious Distress; consider standardized EPDS follow-up and safety plan if status changes.
